Ephemera

ephemera.space
built 2026-11-14 03:32 UTC

An archive of the public Starlink ephemerides, hashed and anchored in Bitcoin, with a daily measure of what the public satellite catalogue can see.

Front page The finding Scored cycles The archive Check it The globe

The archive record

As of 2026-11-14 03:32 UTC. Poller: A (a datacentre host in the EU; the home poller was retired on 3 Oct 2026). 2026 so far; earlier years get their own page once they exist.

The operator side of every comparison comes from files this project caught before they were replaced. Each cycle is hashed file by file into one Merkle root, the root is stamped into the Bitcoin blockchain through OpenTimestamps, and the manifest plus ten files chosen by the root itself are pushed into the Wayback Machine so an independent copy exists that this project does not control.

As of 2026-11-14 03:32 UTC: 237 cycles, 236 complete with roots, 236 anchored in Bitcoin, 17 with a defect in the independent copy. Source bytes archived: 5,386 GB across 2,653,766 files as served. Stored gzipped as 2,214 GB, of which 28 GB is on the poller's disk and 2,186 GB exists only in cold object storage. Cadence holds, meaning a set served longer than nine hours while the poller watched: 20. A further 3 such intervals fell while the poller was down and are not counted as a hold. Poller heartbeat coverage over the last 24 hours: 100.0%. This project exists because SpaceX publishes the feed openly.

Method: built from each cycle's cycle.json, witness.json and ship.json in the poller's spool; coverage is the fraction of the last 24 h's minutes with a watcher heartbeat under 10 minutes old; a cadence hold is a manifest first-seen gap over 9 h; source bytes are the responses as served, stored bytes are the gzipped archive objects the shipper recorded; a block is the lowest in the cycle's own proof; a copy marked found later was located in the Wayback index afterwards and hashed against the record (probe P10). Poller: A (a datacentre host in the EU; the home poller was retired on 3 Oct 2026).

Daily roots. A root over each day's complete cycle roots in first-seen order, joined as raw digests by the same construction as a cycle root, built shortly after midnight UTC and stamped separately.

A cycle still pulling at midnight is left out of that day's root and stays out. It keeps its own cycle root and its own OpenTimestamps proof, so nothing is unwitnessed, but it sits under no daily root.

A row marked found later: Save Page Now answered with an error at the time, so the witness recorded no copy, but the Wayback Machine had made one. On 2026-11-08 the copies were found in its index and hashed against this archive's records. The capture times are the Wayback Machine's own.

A link in the Wayback Machine column can answer 404 for a while, even though the copy was fetched and hashed when it was made. Of the 18 that did on 5 Nov 2026, 15 served the right bytes again on 8 Nov. The likely cause is the Wayback Machine's index catching up, which is an inference.

Cite as: Ryan, K. (2026). Ephemera: an archive of the public Starlink ephemerides and a daily measure of public catalogue visibility. https://ephemera.space, retrieved 2026-11-14 03:32 UTC.

Operator ephemerides are predictions, not observations. Starlink is the only operator with public covariance; other operators enter via CelesTrak SupGP without covariance. Public GP data is too noisy to test sub-metre covariance; the self-consistency scoreboard measures prediction-versus-later-prediction. That scoreboard is not built yet. Inputs are archived by this project and witnessed by OpenTimestamps and the Wayback Machine; they are not re-fetchable from the source after one cycle. Gapped or lost items are printed, never hidden.
